## The same three notes, weighted differently

Play C major as C-E-G, then lift the low C up an octave so E sits at the bottom.
Same three pitch classes. Different weight. The second version feels lighter,
because the bass note is what a chord leans on, and E isn't a settled place to
lean on.

An *inversion* raises one or more low chord tones by an octave. A *voicing* is
the whole choice of register and spacing for every tone in the chord. Root
position puts the root in the bass, first inversion the third, second inversion
the fifth. Those keyboard shapes are also transformations of a sorted array,
which means you can search for one instead of arranging it by hand.

## A greedy search for the nearest chord

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 78
use_synth :piano

define :invert do |notes, count|
  result = notes.sort
  count.times { result = result.drop(1) + [result[0] + 12] }
  result
end

define :distance do |left, right|
  left.zip(right).sum { |a, b| (a - b).abs }
end

define :voice_near do |notes, previous|
  candidates = (0..2).map { |turn| invert(notes, turn) }
  shifted = candidates.flat_map do |candidate|
    [-12, 0, 12].map { |shift| candidate.map { |pitch| pitch + shift } }
  end
  shifted.min_by { |candidate| distance(candidate, previous) }
end

c = chord(:c4, :major).to_a
[c, invert(c, 1), invert(c, 2), [48, 67, 76]].each do |voicing|
  play_chord voicing, release: 1.3
  sleep 2
end

roots = [:c4, :a3, :f3, :g3]
previous = c
roots.each do |root|
  raw = chord(root, :major).to_a
  chosen = voice_near(raw, previous)
  puts "#{root}: #{chosen} movement=#{distance(chosen, previous)}"
  play_chord chosen, release: 1.5
  sleep 2
  previous = chosen
end
```

The first three chords rotate C, E and G through the bass. The fourth spreads
the same harmony across two octaves and opens a hole in the middle of it. Then
the progression runs, and `voice_near` holds each chord near the one you just
heard. Watch the `movement` numbers while you listen.

## Take the search apart

1. Play `raw` in place of `chosen`. Follow the lowest note through both runs.
   The root-position version jumps wherever the root jumps; the searched version
   mostly doesn't.

2. Delete `-12` and `12` from the shift list. With octave displacement gone, the
   search has fewer legal neighbours, and some transitions settle for more
   movement than they need to.

3. Replace `[48, 67, 76]` with `[60, 64, 67]`. Both reduce to the pitch classes
   of C major. One is stretched thin across the keyboard and the other is a
   compact block. Which one still sounds like a single object?

## What the cost function knows, and what it doesn't

Inversion is a cyclic reorder with an octave correction. Move the lowest element
to the end and the array stops ascending, so you add twelve to lift that pitch
above its old neighbours. Every result keeps the original values modulo twelve, so the
chord's identity survives.

`voice_near` is greedy: at each boundary it builds the candidates, scores each
one by total semitone distance from the previous chord, and takes the smallest.
That one preference removes most of the leaps you'd otherwise hear. It knows
nothing about which tone lands in the bass, whether two voices cross, or whether
the result sits in a range anyone can sing. [Lesson 31](31-voice-leading-optimisation-problem.qmd) adds those constraints and
shows you what happens when a low score and good voice leading come apart.

## Take it further

Add a `bass_pitch_class` argument to `voice_near` and reject any candidate whose
lowest note doesn't match it. Render C-F-G-C with C and F in root position, G in
first inversion and the final C in second inversion. Print the movement total
for that constrained path beside the all-root-position baseline. Your version
should move less overall while still landing every bass note you asked for.
